title: How option premiums decay
summary: Time value and theta, why decay speeds up near expiry, and why buying options means working against the clock.
body:
## Two parts of a premium

An option's [[premium]] has two parts. **Intrinsic value** is what the option would be worth if it expired right now: for a call, how far the index is above the [[strike]]; for a put, how far below. **Time value** is everything else: what buyers pay for the chance that the index moves further before [[expiry]].

An [[atm-itm-otm|at-the-money]] option has no intrinsic value. Its whole premium is time value.

## Theta: time value shrinking

As expiry gets closer, there is less time left for a big move, so time value shrinks. This loss is called [[theta-decay|theta decay]]. On expiry day, any remaining time value disappears and the option is worth only its intrinsic value.

If nothing else changes (the index stays where it is and volatility stays the same), an option buyer loses a little every day and a seller gains it.

## Why decay speeds up near expiry

Time value does not shrink in a straight line. With many weeks left, a day passing changes little. With two or three days left, each day takes a much larger share of what remains. Weekly options are always close to expiry, so their decay is fast.

You can see this in Nikasha's results. A bought weekly option held overnight loses value even if the index doesn't move, and the effect is strongest in the last days before expiry.

## Buying options means fighting the clock

When you buy an option, you need the index to move in your direction, far enough and soon enough to beat the decay. A correct view that comes true too slowly can still lose money. That is one reason many option-buying strategies show a low [[win-rate|win rate]]: lots of small losses from decay, offset (or not) by fewer large gains.

When you sell an option, decay works for you, but the risk is reversed: a large, fast move can cost far more than the premium received. The short straddle template carries a prominent warning for this reason.

## Expiry-day behaviour

On expiry day, premiums can swing sharply as the index moves around popular strikes, and time value collapses towards zero by the close. Real expiry-day prices also depend on supply and demand in ways a model can't capture.

Nikasha models premiums with [[black-scholes|Black-Scholes]], using [[india-vix|India VIX]] as the volatility. India VIX reflects 30-day expectations, so the model is least accurate for options very close to expiry. The report notes this, and expiry-day results deserve the most caution.

## What to take away

- Time value is a cost for buyers and an income for sellers.
- Decay accelerates in the final days before expiry.
- Holding a bought option overnight costs time value even on a quiet day.
- Results that rely on expiry-day trades are the least reliable part of any modelled backtest.

title: How to use Nikasha
summary: The three ways in, what happens when you're asked a question, and how to read the review screen and the report.
body:
## Three ways in

Every strategy reaches the same review screen, whichever way you start.

- **Templates** suit you if you're new to options. Each one is explained in plain words, and you can run it with one click on the review screen.
- **Build a strategy** suits you if the rules are in your head. Four short steps (basics, strike, entry, exit) cover everything Nikasha needs. Advanced options stay off unless you switch them on.
- **Upload your strategy** suits you if the rules are written down. Nikasha reads a PDF, Word or text file, or text you paste, and lists what it understood.

## When Nikasha asks you a question

Nikasha never guesses. If a rule is vague ("exit decisively", "a tight [[stop-loss]]"), or a required value is missing, you get one short question at a time, usually with choices. Answering is how the test becomes exactly your strategy rather than someone else's idea of it. Values that are pre-filled, such as the [[lot-size|lot size]], still have to be confirmed by you.

## Reading the review screen

The review screen shows every rule in three columns: the rule, its setting and what it means. Advanced options you didn't use are listed as "Not used", so you can see that nothing was switched on for you. Below the rules are the evaluation settings: the backtest period, each cost with its source, and an optional capital amount. Tick "I've checked the costs and period" once you're happy. The **Evaluate Strategy** button stays disabled, with a list of what is still needed, until everything is complete.

## Reading the report

The report puts risk first. Start with the largest fall from a peak (the [[drawdown]]), the longest [[losing-streak|losing streak]] and the biggest single loss. Only then look at the total result, the [[win-rate|win rate]] and the [[expectancy]].

The breakdowns show when the strategy did well or badly: by year and month, by [[india-vix|India VIX]] level, on trending or sideways days, by weekday, on expiry days, and for calls versus puts. Groups with fewer than ten trades are marked "few trades", because a handful of trades says little.

The overfitting check compares the earlier years with the recent unseen years. If results faded on the unseen years, the rules may have fitted past noise (see [[overfitting]]). The volatility sensitivity shows the same test with India VIX two points lower and higher. If the result changes sign, it depends heavily on how option prices were modelled.

## Trying a change with what-if

Below the report, the what-if sliders change one stop-loss or target value at a time and run the test again on the same period. The panel shows the original next to the changed version, with a sentence such as "With a stop-loss of 25% instead of 30%, this strategy would have…". A small change that flips a profit into a loss is a sign of a fragile rule. **Use these settings** copies the change to the review screen; nothing runs until you press Evaluate again.

## Before you close the tab

Nikasha stores nothing. The report exists only in your open tab. Download the PDF (and the trades CSV if you want the detail) before you close it or refresh the page. Both files include the settings used, the data source and the short disclaimer, so they make sense on their own later.

title: Modelled vs real option prices
summary: Why Nikasha models option prices, Black-Scholes in one paragraph, India VIX as volatility, the limits, and the ±2 VIX check.
body:
## Why prices are modelled

Nikasha has minute-by-minute data for the Nifty 50 index and [[india-vix|India VIX]], but not for individual option contracts. Historical option prices for every strike and expiry are not available in the public data Nikasha uses. So every [[premium]] in a Nikasha report is calculated, not looked up. The report always says "Premiums modelled, not actual".

## Black-Scholes in one paragraph

The [[black-scholes|Black-Scholes]] formula gives a fair price for an option from five inputs: the index level, the [[strike]], the time left to [[expiry]], an interest rate and the volatility. Higher volatility or more time means a higher premium, because a big move becomes more likely. Nikasha calculates the price every minute a simulated position is open, rounds it to the exchange's price step, and uses the minute's high and low index levels to find the highest and lowest premium in that minute for stop-loss and target checks.

## India VIX as the volatility

The formula needs volatility, which can't be observed directly. Nikasha uses India VIX, NSE's index of expected 30-day Nifty volatility, as a stand-in for [[implied-volatility|implied volatility]]. When India VIX was high, modelled premiums are high; when it was low, they are low.

## The limits

Real option prices differ from the model in ways that matter.

- **Skew:** in real markets, options far from the money are usually priced at higher volatility than at-the-money options. The model uses one volatility for every strike, so far strikes are likely underpriced.
- **Expiry day:** India VIX describes the next 30 days. In the last hours before expiry, real premiums behave differently, so expiry-day results are the least reliable.
- **Supply and demand:** real prices react to order flow, news and events. A model can't.
- **Costs and fills:** Nikasha adds slippage and charges, but real fills in fast markets can be worse.

Results that depend on far strikes, expiry-day trades or very short holding times deserve the most caution.

## The ±2 VIX check

Because so much rests on the volatility input, every evaluation is run three times: as modelled, with India VIX two points lower, and two points higher. The report shows all three. If the result changes a lot, or flips between profit and loss, it depends heavily on how option prices were modelled, and the real outcome could easily have been different.

## What to take away

Modelled prices let you compare strategies consistently over many years, which is what a learning tool needs. They are not a record of what real trades would have earned. Treat the numbers as an informed estimate, read the sensitivity section, and remember the badge on every report.

title: What is drawdown?
summary: The fall from a peak, worked through with rupee figures, and why it matters more than the average profit.
body:
## Peak to trough

Add up a strategy's results trade by trade and you get its [[equity-curve|equity curve]]. A **drawdown** is any fall of that curve from its highest point so far. The **maximum drawdown** is the largest such fall in the whole test.

Drawdown is measured from the peak, not from the start. A strategy can be in profit overall and still be in a deep drawdown.

## A worked example

Imagine five trades with these results after costs: +₹10,000, +₹5,000, −₹8,000, −₹6,000, +₹4,000.

- After two trades the equity is ₹15,000. That is the peak.
- After the next two it is ₹1,000. The drawdown is ₹15,000 − ₹1,000 = ₹14,000.
- After the last trade it is ₹5,000, still ₹10,000 below the peak.

The total result is a profit of ₹5,000, but the maximum drawdown was ₹14,000, almost three times as large. Someone following this strategy would have watched most of their gains disappear before the end.

## Why it matters more than the average

The average profit per trade (the [[expectancy]]) tells you what happened on a typical trade. It says nothing about the order of the trades. Drawdown does. It answers a practical question: how much would you have had to sit through, at the worst moment, to get the final result?

Large drawdowns matter for three reasons.

- **Money:** a fall of ₹14,000 needs that much capital behind it. If you entered a capital amount, the report also shows the drawdown as a percentage of it.
- **Recovery:** after a 50% fall, the remaining money has to double just to get back to where it was.
- **Behaviour:** in real trading, deep drawdowns are when people abandon a plan, often at the worst time. A backtest can't feel that, but the number warns you.

## Losing streaks

The report also shows the longest run of losing trades in a row. Losing streaks and drawdowns usually go together: a run of eight small losses can do as much damage as one large loss. A strategy that wins often but has occasional long streaks can still have a painful drawdown.

## How Nikasha shows it

The report puts the maximum drawdown first among the risk figures, before any profit. The drawdown chart sits directly under the equity curve so you can see when the falls happened and how long they lasted. The breakdowns help you see whether the worst periods came in particular years, at particular [[india-vix|India VIX]] levels or on particular kinds of days.

These figures come from simulated trades with modelled option prices on past data. A future drawdown can be larger than any seen in the test.

title: What is overfitting?
summary: Rules that fit past noise, how Nikasha splits tuning years from unseen years, and how to read its overfitting check.
body:
## Rules that fit noise

Past market data is a mix of real patterns and random noise. If you keep adjusting a strategy until it looks good on that data (a slightly different [[stop-loss]], a different [[rsi|RSI]] level, one more filter), you eventually find settings that fit the noise. The result looks excellent on the data used to tune it and disappoints on anything else. This is [[overfitting]].

Overfitting is easy to do without meaning to. Every time you change a rule because of how the last backtest looked, you use up some of the data's ability to tell you the truth.

## The tuning and unseen split

Nikasha checks for this by splitting the test into two parts (see [[in-sample-out-of-sample|in-sample and out-of-sample]]):

- **The tuning period (in-sample):** earlier years, the kind of history anyone designing a strategy today would have looked at. For weekly options this runs from February 2019 to the end of 2023; for monthly options, from the start of the data to the end of 2023.
- **The unseen period (out-of-sample):** from 1 January 2024 to the last date in the data.

The report shows the same figures for both parts side by side.

## What "possibly overfit" means

Nikasha compares the average result per trade ([[expectancy]]) in the two parts:

- If the unseen period's average is below half of the tuning period's, or has the opposite sign, the strategy is flagged **possibly overfit**.
- Otherwise it **held up on unseen data**.

Two situations give no verdict. If either part has fewer than thirty trades, there is too little evidence, and the report says so instead of showing a flag. If the strategy already lost money in the tuning period, there is no good result to test, and the report says that instead.

## How to read it

- A flag is a warning, not proof. Markets change, and an honest strategy can have a weaker recent period.
- Holding up is encouraging, not proof either. Two periods from the same market can still both mislead.
- Look at the breakdowns as well. A strategy whose profits came from one regime or one year is fragile even if the split looks fine.
- Be careful with what-if changes and suggestions. If you tune settings by looking at the whole period, including the unseen years, those years are no longer unseen. Nikasha's suggestions compare variants on both the whole period and the unseen years for this reason.

## A simple habit

Decide your rules first, test them once on the full period, and treat the unseen-period result as the more honest one. If you change rules after seeing results, keep in mind that each change makes the backtest a little more optimistic than reality.

title: Why most strategies fail
summary: Costs, overfitting, changing markets, too few trades and ignored risk — five common reasons a promising backtest disappoints.
body:
## Costs and slippage

Every order has charges: brokerage, [[stt|STT]] on sales, exchange fees, the SEBI fee, stamp duty and GST. On top of that comes [[slippage]], the gap between the price you expect and the price you get. Each is small, but a strategy that trades often pays them many times. A rule that looks profitable before costs can lose money after them.

Nikasha applies every charge to every simulated order and shows the total in the report, so you can see how much of the gross result the costs took away.

## Overfitting to the past

Given enough tries, almost any set of rules can be tuned to look good on past data. The rules end up describing that particular stretch of history, including its random noise, rather than a pattern that repeats. This is [[overfitting]].

The warning sign is a strategy whose results fade on data it wasn't tuned on. Nikasha's overfitting check splits the test into earlier years and recent unseen years and compares the average result per trade. A large drop is flagged as possibly overfit.

## The market changes

Markets move through [[regime|regimes]]: strong trends, quiet sideways stretches, calm and volatile periods. A rule that works in one can fail in another. Trend-following entries, for example, tend to give a string of small losses on sideways days.

The report breaks results down by trend regime and by [[india-vix|India VIX]] level, so you can see whether a strategy depended on one kind of market. A strategy that made all its money in one unusual year deserves a second look.

## Too few trades

A test with fifteen trades says very little. A few lucky results can make the [[win-rate|win rate]] and [[expectancy]] look much better or worse than they really are. The more trades, the more the averages mean.

Nikasha marks breakdown groups with fewer than ten trades as "few trades" and won't call them a best or worst case. The overfitting check needs at least thirty trades in each part before it gives a verdict.

## Ignoring risk

A high win rate can hide a dangerous strategy. Selling options, for example, often wins small amounts many times and then loses a large amount once. The average can look fine while a single bad day wipes out months of gains. That is why the report shows the [[drawdown|maximum drawdown]], the longest losing streak and the largest single loss before any profit figure.

## What this means for reading a backtest

None of these problems can be removed completely, and a good-looking backtest is not evidence that a strategy will work. It is more useful to ask questions of it:

- Do the results survive the costs?
- Did they hold up on the unseen recent years?
- Do they depend on one regime or one year?
- Are there enough trades to say anything?
- Could you have lived through the worst drawdown?

Nikasha's results are simulated on past data with modelled option prices. They describe what would have happened under those assumptions, not what will happen.
